analysis.one_liner: Creates federal crimes for gun trafficking and straw purchasing, with sentences up to 25 years.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by a Chicago congressman and 19 cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote and died in the House Judiciary Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a stand-alone federal crime to buy a gun for someone else (straw purchasing) or to traffic in firearms, punishable by up to 15 years in prison, or 25 years when the guns are destined for violent crime or drug trafficking. It also expands the list of people barred from buying guns, raises penalties for selling guns to those people, makes smuggling guns out of the country a federal crime, and lets prosecutors use wiretaps and racketeering and money-laundering laws against trafficking rings. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of communities affected by gun violence, since the bill aims to cut off the supply of guns to people legally barred from owning them and to trafficking networks that move guns to illegal markets. Police and federal prosecutors also gain new, clearer tools, including wiretap authority and forfeiture of traffickers' profits.

how_it_helps.text: Makes straw purchasing — buying a gun on someone else's behalf, typically for someone who cannot pass a background check — a stand-alone federal crime carrying up to 15 years in prison, and up to 25 years when the buyer knows the gun will be used in a violent or drug-trafficking crime.
Makes it a crime to traffic two or more firearms to a person whose possession would violate federal law, with a 25-year maximum for an organizer running a ring of five or more people.

Expands the list of persons barred from receiving firearms to include anyone who intends to pass a gun to a prohibited person, to use one in a violent or drug-trafficking crime, or to unlawfully export one, and raises the prison maximum for selling to or possessing guns as a prohibited person from 10 to 15 years.

Makes smuggling a firearm or ammunition out of the United States to promote a violent or drug-trafficking crime a federal offense with up to 15 years in prison, and broadens the existing ban on smuggling guns into the country.

Adds the new offenses to the list of crimes for which prosecutors can seek wiretaps, and to federal racketeering and money-laundering statutes, and requires forfeiture of proceeds and property used in trafficking.

analysis.who_pays: People who engage in straw purchasing or trafficking face up to 15 or 25 years in prison and forfeiture of their property. Casual private sellers face new risk, because several offenses turn on what a person 'knows or has reasonable cause to believe' about a buyer. Federal courts and prisons absorb the cost of longer sentences.

drawbacks.text: Several new offenses use a 'reasonable cause to believe' standard rather than actual knowledge, which critics of such bills argue could criminalize a private seller who unknowingly sells to someone headed for trouble, rather than only deliberate traffickers.

The bill raises maximum sentences to 15 and 25 years and directs the Sentencing Commission to increase guidelines for trafficking offenses, adding to federal prison populations — a cost that even supporters of gun enforcement must weigh.

Criminal penalties punish traffickers after the fact and do nothing about the large volume of guns first sold legally by licensed dealers; some gun-safety advocates argue enforcement-only bills leave the upstream legal market untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and specific harm — guns moving through straw buyers and traffickers to people who cannot legally own them — and it pairs new crimes with serious penalties and investigative tools. The main tradeoff is longer prison terms and a 'reasonable cause to believe' standard that could reach beyond ringleaders to peripheral sellers. It is a law-and-order bill rather than a regulation of the gun industry itself, so its effect on the underlying legal gun market would be limited.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee in early 2021, and it sat there until the two-year Congress ended without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush (D-IL) introduced the Gun Trafficking Prohibition Act on January 4, 2021, the opening day of the 117th Congress.
Nineteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and on March 1, 2021 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — is recorded for the remainder of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun trafficking networks and straw buyers are unaffected, since the new crimes were never enacted. The firearms industry and secondary-market sellers avoid any new legal exposure. House members who opposed or simply ignored the bill face no recorded vote on gun trafficking.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Traffickers and the gun status quo

for.name: Rep. Bobby L. Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 117th Congress to create federal gun-trafficking and straw-purchasing crimes.

for.name: 19 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jerrold Nadler (D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after receiving it — no hearing, markup, or vote in the full committee or its crime subcommittee during the two-year Congress.

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority party agenda-setters, 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor at any point in the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican cosponsor is listed. The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists — its fate was decided by Democratic-controlled committee and House agendas, not by a party-line vote.

industries.industry: Firearms dealers and secondary-market private sellers
industries.note: Licensed dealers are exempt from the straw-purchasing offense, but the bill's 'reasonable cause to believe' standards create new legal exposure for private and casual sellers. Enforcement against straw buyers could also reduce the off-the-book sales channel some dealers profit from.

Trafficked guns typically begin as legal retail purchases, so curbing straw purchasing could modestly reduce sales volume; manufacturers face no direct new liability. The industry's interest in maximizing volume runs against the bill's aim of drying up illegal supply.
New 15- and 25-year offenses and sentencing increases mean more federal prosecutions and longer incarceration, expanding demand for prison capacity and court resources.
